Nandana
(‘that which gives joy’)
------------------------------------------
Nandana or Nandanavana is a pleasure garden in इन्द्र’s svargaloka or हेअवेन्. Only those who have controlled their senses and practised अहिṁसा (non-violence) are eligible to enter it.
It is also the name of one of the sons of हिरण्यकशिपु, the demon-king and ड़थेर् of प्रह्लाद, the famous devotee of Lord विष्णु. He was a devotee of शिव and ruled over the श्वेतद्वीप. (See ŚVETA-DVĪPA.) Later on, he was absorbed into शिव’s retinue.

Nandapaṇḍita
------------------------------------------
Nandapaṇḍita (circa A.

-1630), son of Rāmapaṇḍita Devaśarma, was a descendant of लक्ष्मीधर, belonging to Bidar (now in North Karnataka). He probably lived mostly in काशी where he composed his voluminous works on the धर्मशास्त्रस्. His another name was विनायक.
He was patronised by several rich persons from different parts of India, like Paramānanda of the Sahagila family, Harivaṁśavarma of the महेन्द्र family and Keśavanāyaka of मधुरा.
His most famous work is the Dattaka-mīmāṁsā which had been considered as an authority even by the British rulers of India while settling family disputes of the Hindus.
Out of the thirteen works attributed to him, a few many be mentioned here:
Vidvanmanoharā on Parāśarasmṛti; Pramitākṣarā, a commentary on the Mitā-kṣarā of विज्ञानेश्वर (12th century A. D.); Śrāddhakalpalatā; Smṛtisindhu and its summary Tattvamuktāvalī.
The Dattakamīmāṁsā has his own commentary.
Though नन्दपण्डित generally follows the Mitākṣarā, he sometimes differs strongly from it with regard to succession and a few other matters.

Nanda
------------------------------------------
Nanda was the chieftain of the cowherds at the village गोकुल. He was an intimate friend of Vasudeva, the ड़थेर् of Śrī कृष्ण and बलराम.
He and his wife यशोदा were, in a previous life, वसुस् (a race of semi-gods) known as Droṇa and Dharā. They had performed severe austerities to get God as their son. A voice from the void had assured them that God would bless them in a future life with his childish pranks (as their foster-son) bringing great joy.
Śrī कृष्ण and बलराम spent their childhood days with नन्द and यशोदा until they left for मथुरा for good. During this period, Śrī कृष्ण saved नन्द from drowning in the river यमुना.
Many years later, नन्द, when he learnt that Śrī कृष्ण and बलराम had come to Syamantapañcaka (same as कुरु-क्षेत्र) to take a dip in the holy lake there on a solar एच्लिप्से day, hurried to the place with plenty of ड़ोओद् and other useful things. Śrī कृष्ण is said to have honoured नन्द and यशोदा in many ways and also taught spiritual wisdom to the गोपीस् who too had come to meet him.
See also BALARĀMA and KṚṢṆA.

Nandotsava
------------------------------------------
Śrī कृष्ण was born on the midnight of Śrāvaṇa-कृष्ण-aṣṭamī (the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, generally in August). He was immediately transported from the prison of कṁस, the tyrant, to the होउसे of नन्द, the chief of the cow-herds at गोकुल. The next day known as श्रीकृष्ण-jayantī or simply Jayantī, was celebrated by नन्द with great joy and fervour. Hence that day—the Jayantī—is also called ‘Nandotsava’.
See also JANMĀṢṬAMĪ.

Nānak, Guru
(A.

-1539)
------------------------------------------
Guru Nānak is the founder of सिखिस्म्, the youngest of the great religions of the world.
Whether सिखिस्म् is an offshoot of हिन्दुइस्म् or a completely independent religion, there is no gainsaying the fact that the Sikhs, under their inspired Gurus, fought bravely with the alien hordes, many of them laying down their lives too, in the process, to protect the Hindu society and save हिन्दुइस्म्.
गुरु.jpg" src="http://eoh.rkmathbangalore.org/public/images/thumbs/N%C4%81nak,%20Guru.jpg" alt="Guru Nānak">Guru NānakGuru Nānak was born in A.

at Talwandi (now known as Nānkānā Sāhib) which is 48 kms. (30 miles) to the south-east of Lahore, now in Pakistan, as the only son of Mahitā Kāū (the village accountant) and Tṛptā.
Nānak proved to be a precocious child, exhibiting such powers as speaking about various subjects of religion and philosophy at the age of five, and learning all the alphabet in just one day as also composing poems, at seven!
Even as he was being invested with the यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread), he composed a poem that expounded the spiritual significance of the same.
He was married at the tender age of 14—as was the custom during those days—to Sulakkhaṇī, daughter of Mūlcand Coṇā of Baṭālā. He had two sons from her, the first one being Śrīcand, the founder of the Udāsī sect.
All efforts by his ड़थेर् to get him settled in the life of this world failed. His brother-in-law, living at Sultanpur took him under his care and got him employed as a store-keeper of the Muslim head, Daulat Khān. Though he performed his allotted duties very well and won the confidence of his boss, he used to distribute most of his salary among the poor people.
During this period, he suddenly disappeared into a nearby forest and spent three days in deep meditation. He heard a divine voice that commanded him to show compassion to the suffering humanity and appointed him as the गुरु (or spiritual guide) for the same.
It was at Sultanpur that Nānak was joined by Mardānā (A.

-1534), an old friend of his boyhood days, from his native village. He was a good musician and thenceforward, became an inseparable companion of the गुरु, singing his compo-sitions to the accompaniment of rabāb (rebeck), a stringed instrument similar to violin.
Soon after his return from the forest hide-out where he had had a high mystical experience, he gifted away all his belongings, wore the dress of a mendicant (that resembled the robe of a Hindu jogi as also that of a Muslim fakīr) and started on a journey of the country to spread his spiritual message that could bring about the union of hearts of all, irrespective of their religion and beliefs.
Apart from the various important centres of Hindu पिल्ग्रिमगे in India, Nānak visited Mecca, Medina and Baghdad too.
Nānak spread his teachings mostly through devotional and didactic songs—all his own compositions—to the accompaniment of rabāb played by Mardānā.
Conversion of a robber Mardan Shekh to सिखिस्म् after he repented for his sins due to Nānak’s teachings, teaching some ब्राह्मणस् the futility of dry and meaning-less rituals, vanquishing quite a few pundits in philosophical disputations, boldly refusing to cow down before the Mughal emperor Babur’s threats ordering him to become a Muslim, are some of the extraordinary doings attributed to him by his biographers.
After appointing Aṅgad (A.
-1552)—known earlier as Lenā—as his successor, गुरु Nānak left for his heavenly abode in A.

. When the shroud covering his body was removed, the body had disappeared, leaving a heap of flowers. The Hindus and the Muslims shared the same and built separately a temple and a mausoleum in his honour.
Guru Nānak’s teachings are contained in the Japjī, comprising the Mūlmantra followed by 38 stanzas, all composed by him.
The Mūlmantra describes God as the Only One, the Infinite One, the Eternal, the Spirit, the Creator. He is All-pervading, the Sovereign Lord, the Harmonious, the Immortal, the Unincarnated and the Self-existent. He is worshipped by the grace of the गुरु.
The Japjī deals with five stages through which an individual सोउल् has to pass, on its way to the realisation of God.
Meditation on God at dawn and the importance of God’s grace are also stressed greatly.
Guru Nānak seems to have attempted a balanced combination of the best teachings of हिन्दुइस्म् and Islam and make his religion simple as also practicable for the common masses. His eldest son Śrīcand (A.

-1629) who was also a highly evolved spiritual सोउल्, started his own monastic sect (the Udāsī sect).
See also SIKHISM.

Nandipurāṇa
------------------------------------------
The purāṇas—the mythological lore of Hinduism—contain a lot of material on the subjects generally dealt with in the dharmaśāstra literature. They have been traditionally grouped under two heads: The Mahāpurāṇas and the उपपुराणस्, each of them being 18 in number.
The Nandipurāṇa—also called Nandapurāṇa—assigned to the latter group, is probably lost now, though a large number of its verses have been quoted in the Kalpataru of लक्ष्मीधर (12th century A. D.) and Aparārka of Aparāditya (also of 12th century A. D.).
Some of the interesting subjects dealt with in it are: ārogyadāna by starting and running free hospitals; vidyādāna by running pāṭhaśālas or schools; abstention from meat-eating.
This purāṇa was probably composed during the 8th or the 9th century A. D.

Nandanār
------------------------------------------
If orthodoxy and social hierarchy divided the Hindu society, often causing great discontent among the lower classes and alienating them from the aristocrats, the भक्ति Movement started by the great mystics and saints of India united all—irrespective of caste and class—into one family of devotees of God.
One such great saint hailing from the Tamil country was नन्दनार्. He belonged to the untouchable group of castes. Being an ardent devotee of Lord शिव, he often longed to go to the holy city of चिदम्बरम् (or Chidambaram) and have a darśan (seeing the image) of the Lord there. After months of hesitation he reached the place. But, recalling the greatness of the city and his own low-birth status, he considered himself unworthy to enter it. Though he remained outside its walls, his yearning for the Lord became so intense that the ब्राह्मण priests were commanded by the Lord शिव himself to bring his devotee into the temple. When this was done, नन्दनार् is said to have fallen into an ecstatic state.
Very little is known of his life and times.

Nandi
------------------------------------------
Anyone visiting a temple of Lord शिव will not miss the image of a reclining bull, generally facing the शिवलिङ्ग in the sanctum. This bull is called by various names such as नन्दि, Nandīśvara or Nandikeśvara. It is the वाहन or mount of Lord शिव even as the गरुड (eagle) is the वाहन of Lord विष्णु.
There are several stories in the पुराणस् about this Nandikeśvara.
A sage, Śālaṅkāyana by name, performed austerities to get a worthy son. Pleased with him, विष्णु appeared before him; and lo! a baby figure exactly like शिव emerged out of him. This was Nandikeśvara.
According to another legend, the sage Śilāda performed a यज्ञ to get a son who would be immortal. A brilliant lad, resembling शिव, suddenly appeared from the inner apartment of his होउसे. He was Nandikeśvara. Another story states that sage who performed severe austerities on the Muñjavān peak of मन्दर mountain was made the chief of his attendants by शिव, who gave him the name Nandīśvara or Nandikeśvara. Iconographically, नन्दि-keśvara is shown either as a small reclining bull facing the शिवलिङ्ग in the sanc-tum or as a big bull in a separate मण्डप (hall) with elaborate workmanship, either facing the main shrine or the main gate.
In many temples, especially in Tamil Nadu, Nandikeśvara is shown in the human form, either with a bull’s head or a human head with जटामुकुट. (See JAṬĀMUKUṬA.) He may have three eyes and four arms, the back hands holding परशु (axe) and mṛga (deer) and the front two folded in supplication (añjalimudrā).
Nandikeśvara is said to have cursed रावण to be destroyed by monkeys when he once ridiculed him near the कैलास mountain (Rāmāyaṇa, Uttarakāṇḍa 16).
The image of Nandikeśvara should be stationed at the dakṣiṇadvāra or southern door of the temple.
See also ADHIKĀRANANDI.

Nandaka
(‘that which gives joy [to the gods]’)
------------------------------------------
All the deities of the Hindu pantheon have their āyudhas or weapons and other objects, normally held in their hands.
Though Mahāviṣṇu (or विष्णु) is usually shown with शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus) in his four hands, he has four more accessories. They are: नन्दक (a sword), शार्ङ्ग (a bow), मुसल (mace) and वनमाला (garland of wild flowers).
All these eight are worshipped keeping them in the eight directions.
